conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling nauseous and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since last night. I had dinner like normal, but then I started feeling sick and threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you notice any blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It looked kind of like coffee grounds. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can mean there’s some irritation or bleeding in the stomach or esophagus. Given your history of gastroparesis and diabetes, this isn’t uncommon during a flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had anything to eat today. My stomach just feels full and heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to start you on IV fluids to rehydrate you and give you some anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still take my insulin even though I’m not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. You must never skip your insulin, even if you're not eating. We’ll adjust the doses based on your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered some blood tests and a chest X-ray to make sure there’s no infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a chest X-ray before, right? For the last admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this one looks similar—no pneumonia or pneumothorax. Your heart size is normal, and the gastric pacer leads are still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. We also did an abdominal X-ray. It shows your bowels aren’t blocked, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been admitted a few times for this. Is this just another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a gastroparesis flare, yes. We’re giving you your usual metoclopramide and adding compazine for nausea control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard sometimes people make themselves throw up. I don’t do that, just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for saying that. We just need to understand all possibilities. Your labs show mild dehydration and slightly high white blood cells, but no infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure? It’s usually high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit elevated today—167 over 84. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your lisinopril dose may be adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I didn’t vomit last night, but I still don’t feel like eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to try starting you on small sips of ginger ale and see if you can tolerate toast later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My mouth is still dry, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing IV fluids to help with that. Your blood sugar has been stable, which is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a urine test last night. Was there anything wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed mixed bacteria, but that’s likely from contamination. No sign of a urinary infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down toast and applesauce yesterday. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We want to make sure you can keep food and meds down. We’re also adjusting your medications for long-term protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your lisinopril to 7.5 mg daily to protect your kidneys from diabetes damage. And we’re starting a baby aspirin for heart protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember starting those last time. Are they working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s important to stay on them. We’re also giving you both oral and rectal compazine in case nausea comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The rectal one? I’ve never used that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s helpful if you can’t keep pills down. It works well for nausea and is safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’ve had two meals without vomiting. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling more like myself. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to do well. We’ll write your discharge orders today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the compazine as prescribed. Avoid large meals, soda, or eating too fast. And never skip insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it doesn’t help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re stable, eating, and taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Make sure you take the pantoprazole daily for your esophagitis. It helps reduce stomach acid and irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll start it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Keep your blood sugar in check—it helps prevent these flares. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel okay. A bit tired, but no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Remember—small, frequent meals. No skipping insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And take the new meds every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we reviewed your labs and imaging. Everything supports a gastroparesis flare with no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the coffee ground vomit wasn’t serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests mild bleeding, likely from esophagitis or a small tear from vomiting. The pantoprazole will help heal that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—any questions before you go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. All set.
